fields.title: Polka: March 1 deadline, a quarter's worth of work
fields.summary: The contract with the retail chain depends on a single date. Decide how to plan the delivery.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you plan these seven weeks, and what will go into each release?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional inventory app for small stores. The team has four people, with releases every two weeks.
fields.brief/context: Today is January 10. The Gastronom retail chain (40 stores, 38% of Polka's revenue) will renew their contract on March 1—on the condition that data export to their accounting system works. Meanwhile, version 2.0 is ready for a full rollout, and the backlog has piled up.
fields.brief/objective: Plan the work so that the contract is renewed on March 1.
fields.brief/constraints: Seven weeks, four people. Everything won't fit.
fields.brief/task: Choose a plan and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A hard deadline is planned backward, not forward
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When the cost of delay drops off a cliff on a specific date, work is planned backward with a buffer, and dependencies on external teams are turned into milestones with triggers and owners. The second rule of this block is to never combine independent changes: a release containing both an integration and a new version can neither be rolled back nor properly evaluated.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
A. Export to Gastronom's accounting system. Deadline March 1, otherwise the contract won't be renewed—38% of revenue. Dev estimate: 2 weeks, but they will send the export format "at the end of January."

B. Transitioning all clients to version 2.0. Ready, tested internally. Transition estimate: 2 weeks of team work plus support.

C. Scanner doesn't read crumpled barcodes. Affects 40% of inventories, cashiers enter codes manually, adding 40 minutes per inventory. Estimate: 3 days.

D. Export for accounting, requested by two stores. Estimate: 2 weeks. They currently reconcile manually and manage fine.

E. Dark theme, requested twice. Estimate: 3 days.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: What is known about the export
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Gastronom's accounting system is an in-house development by their IT department of two people.

They promise to send the export format "at the end of January." There is no reply to the December 20 email yet.

They have no staging environment: testing must be done in production, by agreement during off-hours.

It is undecided whose version of stock levels is the source of truth. Their IT believes it's their system; your stock levels are collected from the in-store scanner.

It is undecided what happens if their system is unavailable: currently, the export project simply doesn't retry sending data.

Last time, a similar integration for another client took three weeks instead of two due to date formats.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Version 2.0 is rewritten: new inventory screen, faster, supports multiple warehouses.

The discrepancy report they are used to looks different and is located elsewhere.

The supplier directory from 1.x is not migrated yet—only two developers know this, and it's not in the transition plan. Re-entering it manually takes about two hours per store.

No rollback to 1.x is planned after the transition: data is written to the new structure.

Support: currently one person, overwhelmed on release days.

Last year, the transition to 1.5 was done on a single date: 12 out of 40 stores asked to roll back in the first week.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Four people: two developers, a tester, and you. A designer is available for a quarter of their time, shared with another product.

From January 10 to March 1 — seven weeks. One of the developers is on vacation from February 16 to 22; the vacation was approved half a year ago.

Releases are every two weeks, on Thursdays.

Support is shared across all clients: 40 Gastronom stores plus 60 stores of other clients.

Last quarter, the team planned 100% of their time for tasks; in reality, about 20% went to unplanned work.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Plan based on deadline and risks
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Count backward from March 1, manage the format risk with a trigger and a backup plan, integrate with a decision on data ownership, and roll out 2.0 in phases only after the contract is signed.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Counting backward sets a hard frame: two weeks for the export plus a one-week buffer for the date format (which took an extra week last time)—meaning you need the format by February 5, not "at the end of January."
You write an email to Gastronom's IT with a date and a trigger: if the format isn't ready by February 5, you escalate to their director. The format arrives on February 3.
Before starting, you resolve two questions: stock levels are yours, prices are theirs; if their system is down, exports queue up and retry instead of getting lost. Both answers took just one meeting and prevented future arguments.
You do C (three days, 40% of inventories) in the first sprint—this also boosts Gastronom's mood before negotiations.
You start rolling out 2.0 in phases after March 1: five stores first, then a larger group. During the first wave, the unmigrated supplier directory issue surfaces and is fixed before the second wave.
The contract is renewed on February 28. D and E are not done.
Compromise: 2.0 was delayed by a month, which felt like a loss of momentum to the team.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Bundle everything into a single release by March 1
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Export, 2.0, and the scanner fix are released together on February 26: one big release, one update for clients, saving on deployment overhead.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The export format arrives on February 9, a week later than expected. There is no buffer in the plan.
The developer's vacation starting February 16 subtracts another week from the remaining two.
Everything is released at once on February 26. The export works, but along with it, all 40 Gastronom stores get 2.0—with the unmigrated supplier directory and no way to roll back.
Support goes down on day one: questions about the new version and discrepancy investigations happen at the same time, making it impossible to tell what caused what.
The contract is renewed, but with a quarterly probation period and a demand for a stability plan.
Compromise: two independent changes were released on the same day, so neither could be rolled back or evaluated separately.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Start with 2.0 as the most valuable item
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: 2.0 is ready and brings the most value to all clients. Transition everyone in January, and build the export in February—two weeks should be enough.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The transition takes three and a half weeks instead of two: the supplier directory doesn't migrate, which is discovered at the tenth store.
Support is busy with the transition all of January and half of February.
Export development starts on February 12. The format is available by then, but the date format diverges again—just like last time—and the developer is on vacation starting the 16th.
On March 1, the export is not ready. Gastronom renews the contract for one month instead of a year and requests a written plan.
Compromise: priority was chosen based on the size of the benefit, ignoring the fact that one task has a cost of delay that drops off on a specific date, while the other does not.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Sort by cost of delay and go down the list
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Calculate WSJF for all five items, get the order C -> A -> B -> D -> E, and assign it to the team.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The order is correct, and the priority debate is settled in an hour—the best outcome of this approach.
However, three gaps remain in the plan: no one pushes for the export format because the "end of January" deadline sounds early enough; the question of stock ownership surfaces during development and costs five days of emailing; the transition to 2.0 is scheduled for a single date, just like last year.
The export is ready by February 27, and the contract is renewed.
The transition to 2.0 in March repeats last year's story: 11 stores ask to roll back, but rollback is impossible.
Compromise: priority was calculated correctly, but risks, integration agreements, and the transition plan were left out.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Work order chosen by importance rather than cost of delay and size
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Release is assembled from ready-made pieces and does not allow completing the task end-to-end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Risk is identified, but lacks a trigger, response plan, and owner
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Undecided whose data is the source of truth and what happens if one side is unavailable
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Transition is planned as a single switchover date without phases or rollback options
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Training is reduced to instructions instead of on-the-job guidance
